At 4:17 in the morning, the city forgot what it was supposed to be.

The traffic lights continued their patient changing—red, green, yellow—though no cars passed beneath them. Storefronts held their blank reflections. A newspaper lifted itself from the gutter, turned once in the wind, and settled again beside a crushed paper cup.

Mara was awake because the radiator had begun knocking.

It had been knocking for years, but usually in the background, one of the ordinary noises of the apartment: pipes, refrigerator, upstairs footsteps, the occasional sigh of the building settling into itself. Tonight the sound came from inside the wall with a strange urgency.

Knock.

Knock-knock.

Pause.

Knock.

She lay in bed listening. The room was dark except for the blue numbers on the alarm clock. She had been dreaming of a beach she had never visited. In the dream, someone had written her name in the sand, but the tide had erased everything except the first letter.

She got up.

The floorboards were cold. In the kitchen, she filled the kettle and stood at the window while it heated. Across the street, the old tailor’s shop was dark. Above it, in the apartment where Mr. Vale used to live, a single light burned.

Mr. Vale had died in February. Mara had never met him, though she had seen him from time to time: a narrow man in a gray coat, carrying groceries in a canvas bag. After his death, his apartment remained empty. The light had not come on since the funeral.

Now it flickered.

Mara set down her cup.

There are moments, she thought, when the world makes a small mistake. A bird flies indoors. A clock strikes thirteen. A light appears in a dead man’s window. The sensible response is to look away.

Instead, she put on her coat.

Outside, the air had the sharp, metallic smell that comes before snow. The street was empty. Her shoes clicked against the pavement, each sound traveling farther than it should. She crossed to the tailor’s shop and entered through the side door, which she knew did not lock properly. The hallway smelled of dust, old cooking, and the wet wool of winter.

On the third floor, Mr. Vale’s door stood slightly open.

Mara pushed it.

“Hello?”

No answer.

The apartment looked preserved rather than abandoned. A chair stood beside a table set for one. A pair of glasses rested on an open book. There were photographs on the walls, most of them turned face-down except for one: a young woman sitting on a stone wall, squinting into the sun.

Mara stepped closer.

The woman looked familiar.

Not familiar as in someone Mara had seen before, but familiar in the way a forgotten song can be familiar. Her hair was dark and cut to her shoulders. She wore a white dress. One hand rested on her knee; the other held a small red flower.

Behind Mara, the door clicked shut.

She turned.

Mr. Vale was standing in the hallway.

He looked exactly as he had in the street, except paler, as if the light had passed through him and found nothing to stop it.

“You shouldn’t be here,” he said.

“I’m sorry.”

“It’s all right. People are always arriving somewhere they shouldn’t.”

Mara could think of nothing to say. The radiator knocked in the wall behind her.

Mr. Vale looked toward it. “That’s the trouble.”

“What trouble?”

“It has been trying to tell me something for forty years.”

He walked into the room. The floor did not creak beneath him.

Mara glanced again at the photograph. “Who is she?”

“My sister.”

“What happened to her?”

“She left.”

“Where did she go?”

Mr. Vale smiled, but there was no happiness in it. “That is what I’ve been trying to find out.”

He took the photograph from the wall and turned it over. On the back, in faded blue ink, was an address.

Mara read it.

It was her address.

For a moment, neither of them moved.

“That’s impossible,” she said.

“Most important things are.”

The radiator knocked again. This time, the pattern seemed almost clear.

Three knocks. Pause. Two knocks. Pause. Three.

Mr. Vale crossed to the wall and placed his hand against it. “She was supposed to meet me here,” he said. “The night she disappeared. I waited until morning. Then I waited another day. Eventually, I understood that waiting can become a kind of life.”

Mara looked at the photograph. “Why would she have my address?”

“Perhaps it wasn’t your address then.”

She thought of the apartment she had rented six months earlier, the low rent, the landlord who had avoided her questions. She thought of the first night, when she had found a small red flower pressed between the pages of a book left on the kitchen shelf.

She had thrown it away.

“I don’t understand.”

“No,” said Mr. Vale. “But you may.”

He lifted a loose panel beneath the window. Behind it was a narrow cavity in the wall. Inside lay a tin box, blackened with age.

Mara opened it.

There were letters, dozens of them, tied with string. Every envelope bore the same name: Elian.

Her name.

Not Mara.

Elian.

The radiator stopped knocking.

In the sudden silence, the apartment seemed to expand around them. The walls receded. The ceiling rose. Somewhere far away, a train passed through the city, though there were no tracks nearby.

Mr. Vale touched the letters. “She called you that.”

“Who?”

“Your mother.”

Mara stared at him.

She had never known her mother. There had been a fire in a village she could barely remember, a woman’s hand pulling her through smoke, a red flower pinned to a white dress. Afterward, she had been raised by strangers who told her very little and changed the subject whenever she asked.

The room blurred.

Mr. Vale’s voice became distant. “She left you with me for one night. She said she would return. I was young. I thought all promises had an expiration date.”

Mara opened the first letter.

The handwriting was thin and slanted.

My little Elian,  
If you are reading this, then I have failed to come back in time.

She stopped.

Outside, snow began to fall. It moved through the streetlights in slow, bright spirals, each flake briefly visible before vanishing into the dark.

Mr. Vale was fading.

“Wait,” Mara said. “You can’t leave.”

“I have been leaving for a long time.”

“Where will you go?”

He looked toward the photograph, toward the young woman with the red flower. “Wherever she went.”

Then he was gone.

The light in the apartment went out.

Mara stood alone with the letters.

By dawn, she had read every one.

Her mother had not abandoned her. She had been searching. She had written from cities whose names no longer existed, from hospitals, train stations, borrowed rooms. She had asked strangers to deliver the letters. None had reached Mara.

The final letter contained only one sentence:

I am sorry the world made us late.

Years later, Mara would think often about that sentence. She would wonder whether lateness was a flaw in the world or merely another form of distance. She would keep the letters in a wooden box beside her bed. She would learn to listen when the radiator knocked.

And sometimes, just before morning, when the snow made the city quiet and the traffic lights changed for no one, she would see a woman in a white dress standing across the street.

The woman would raise one hand.

Mara would raise hers.

Neither of them would move closer.

But neither would leave.
